summary: Provides the XDR description for NFS version 4 minor version 1, the formal data encoding used for its messages.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the exact blueprint of how the file-sharing messages are laid out.

questions: where is the nfs 4.1 xdr description
how do i extract the nfs xdr file
what is the nfs compound operation
subtitle: The machine-readable XDR file that spells out every message format in NFS version 4.1.

tldr.problem: NFSv4.1 defines many operations and data types, and implementers need one exact, compilable description of how each is laid out on the wire.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5662 prints the complete XDR description of NFSv4.1 inside the document, with every line marked so a tiny shell script can extract it into a ready-to-compile file.
tldr.outcome: It adds no new protocol rules. The behaviour lives in RFC 5661, and this RFC is the formal data definition that goes with it.

today: RFC 5662 is a Proposed Standard from January 2010 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Read it together with RFC 5661, which defines the NFSv4.1 protocol this XDR describes.

sections.title: What This Document Provides
sections.content:
RFC 5662 provides the External Data Representation Standard (XDR) description for Network File System version 4 (NFSv4) minor version 1. The XDR language itself is defined in RFC 4506, and the protocol that the description belongs to is NFSv4.1 in RFC 5661.

Nearly all of the document, from page 2 to page 72, is this one XDR description. The few sentences around it say that it covers NFSv4.1 and that the security and IANA considerations are those of RFC 5661.
sections.plainLanguage: This document does not explain how file sharing works. It only gives the exact shapes of the messages, and a separate book explains how to use them.

sections.title: Extracting the Machine-Readable File
sections.content:
The description is written so that a reader can turn it into a ready-to-compile file. Every line of XDR in the document starts with the sentinel ///. A one-line shell script, grep '^ *///' | sed 's?^ */// ??' | sed 's?^ *///$??', keeps only those lines and strips the leading white space and the sentinel.

If the script is saved as extract.sh and the RFC text as spec.txt, then sh extract.sh < spec.txt > nfs4_prot.x produces the file. The XDR description and the extraction scripts are Code Components under the IETF Trust's legal provisions, so they carry their own license text, which the XDR file repeats at the top.
sections.plainLanguage: Every line of the blueprint wears a special stamp. A simple filter that keeps only stamped lines gives you the clean blueprint a computer can read.

sections.title: Constants, Basic Types and Structures
sections.content:
The file begins with size limits and basic typedefs. Examples include NFS4_FHSIZE (128, the maximum size of a file handle), NFS4_VERIFIER_SIZE (8), NFS4_OPAQUE_LIMIT (1024) and NFS4_SESSIONID_SIZE (16). Names, paths and strings are built on utf8string, and file offsets and lengths use 64-bit unsigned types.

Next come enumerations and structures. File types are listed in nfs_ftype4, from NF4REG (1, a regular file) and NF4DIR (2) to NF4NAMEDATTR (9). The time structure nfstime4 holds a 64-bit seconds and a 32-bit nseconds. A stateid4 has a 32-bit seqid and 12 opaque bytes.

The description also covers access control entries and their flags and masks, mode bits, file system locations, and the layouttype4 values for file, object and block layouts. A long block of numbered constants such as FATTR4_SUPPORTED_ATTRS (0) and FATTR4_TYPE (1) names the file attributes, and the last one shown is FATTR4_FS_CHARSET_CAP (76).
sections.plainLanguage: First the blueprint lists the sizes of its boxes and the kinds of things a box can hold, such as a file, a folder or a shortcut. Then it shows how to put several boxes together to make bigger ones.

sections.title: Operations, COMPOUND and the Two Programs
sections.content:
Requests are bundled with COMPOUND. The argument structure COMPOUND4args has a tag, a minorversion and an argarray of operations, and the reply COMPOUND4res returns a status, the tag and a resarray of results. The enumeration nfs_opnum4 assigns each operation a number, for example OP_ACCESS = 3, OP_READ = 25 and OP_WRITE = 38.

NFSv4.1 adds operations numbered 40 to 58, including OP_EXCHANGE_ID (42), OP_CREATE_SESSION (43), OP_SEQUENCE (53) and OP_RECLAIM_COMPLETE (58). The SEQUENCE arguments carry a session ID, a sequence ID, a slot ID, a highest slot ID and a flag saying whether to cache the reply.

The server side is program NFS4_PROGRAM, program number 100003, version 4, with two procedures: NFSPROC4_NULL (0) and NFSPROC4_COMPOUND (1). A second program, NFS4_CALLBACK (0x40000000), lets the server call the client, with CB_NULL (0) and CB_COMPOUND (1). Its callback operations include OP_CB_GETATTR (3) and OP_CB_RECALL (4). A comment in the file explains that the callback program number is in the transient range, because the client assigns the exact number and gives it to the server using the SETCLIENTID operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking the file server one small question at a time, the client can hand over a whole list of jobs in one envelope. The server answers with a list of results, and it can also knock on the client's door when it needs something.

sections.title: Error Codes
sections.content:
The enumeration nfsstat4 lists every status value. NFS4_OK is 0. Values from 1 to 70 include (for example NFS4ERR_PERM = 1 and NFS4ERR_NOENT = 2), and a comment asks that value 19 never be allocated because it meant something different in NFSv3. Protocol-specific errors begin at 10001 with NFS4ERR_BADHANDLE.

A marker in the file reads "NFSv4.1 errors start here", and the new codes run from NFS4ERR_BADIOMODE (10049) to NFS4ERR_DELEG_REVOKED (10087); the file notes that 10073 is unused. Some of these concern sessions, such as NFS4ERR_BADSESSION and NFS4ERR_BADSLOT, and others concern request and reply size limits, such as NFS4ERR_REQ_TOO_BIG and NFS4ERR_REP_TOO_BIG.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, the server answers with a numbered note saying what happened, like "no such file" or "you may not do that". The blueprint lists every possible note and its number.

sections.title: Carrying NFSv4.0 Along
sections.content:
The RFC says the description deliberately includes operations and other features of NFSv4.0 that do not apply to NFSv4.1, so that implementations supporting both minor versions can use one file. The text derives from the definitions in RFC 3530 and RFC 5661, as the file's own note states.

The file marks leftovers clearly. Operations OP_OPEN_CONFIRM (20), OP_RENEW (30), OP_SETCLIENTID (35), OP_SETCLIENTID_CONFIRM (36) and OP_RELEASE_LOCKOWNER (39) carry the comment "Mandatory not-to-implement". The error NFS4ERR_RESOURCE is annotated as not a valid error in NFSv4.1.
sections.plainLanguage: The new blueprint keeps a few old pieces so that old and new builders can share one set of drawings. Some of those old pieces are stamped "do not use".

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: This RFC defines no behaviour of its own, so it has nothing separate to say about security or IANA. Both sections simply refer the reader to the Security Considerations and IANA Considerations of RFC 5661.
sections.plainLanguage: Because this document is only the drawings, the safety rules are in the main instruction book, and this document points you there.
